IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00923

Yet we also have to recognise that the devout readers who used it for centuries would have found it difficult to accept that the most important meaning of Scripture is what we now call its “natural and historical” meaning. Beneath their awkwardness and their sometimes irritating tricks of interpretation, we must try to discover what they were really seeking. Perhaps we are making a different mistake of our own when we fail to ask the basic question: what makes understanding possible? In what kind of space does it unfold? In what kind of time does it happen?
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00924

How we answer these questions—we have already tried to answer the first two—determines whether we confuse allegory with symbol or keep them distinct. Among all the People of the Book, we can distinguish two broad tendencies. Some interpreters sought meaning but never went beyond allegory; they are most often found within official religious institutions. Others genuinely sought and practised spiritual interpretation; they are most often found outside the established, majority traditions. There is a reason for this difference. Allegory is harmless. Spiritual meaning can be revolutionary.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00925

Allegorical interpretation often feels artificial because, in the end, it tells us something we could have said without the allegory. It works within fixed boundaries. Those boundaries exclude not only the return of spontaneous, personal prophetic inspiration but also the possibility of a prophetic way of interpreting Scripture. Anything already condemned as “heresy” is unavailable from the outset.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00926

The interpreter’s vision is closed to the pleroma—the fullness of the spiritual world—to the events that take place there, and to all those realities that can reach our awareness only through symbols. An allegory merely restates something already clear to consciousness, something that could always be known and expressed in another way. That is why it can seem both unnecessary and contrived. Allegory can move in several directions, but all those directions stay on the same level of awareness and of our understanding of what exists.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00927

Spiritual interpretation through symbols works differently. It preserves both the words of the text and their hidden meaning—the outward (zahir) and the inward (batin). Only when both are held together can the literal words become transparent to another world. And that other world becomes visible through the words themselves, not by doing away with them.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00928

When the written words become a symbol, they are not a disposable disguise for something we could easily say more directly. They are the only, and the best, expression available for beings and events that have not yet been put into words: realities dimly sensed, things that have not reached ordinary awareness or may never fully be able to reach it. A symbol can never exhaust the mystery to which it points. Explaining a symbol, therefore, does not abolish it or make it useless, as an explanation might do with an allegory.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00929

We must return to it and uncover its meaning again and again; we must make its meaning real in our own experience. We understand symbols by moving down or up through different levels of being, through deeper levels of consciousness or higher levels beyond ordinary consciousness.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00930

That is why Swedenborg’s interpretation, as we saw in § 2, draws out spiritual meaning while expressly rejecting allegorical interpretation. It does not abolish the literal meaning or what he calls the apparentiae reales, the “real appearances.” Instead it makes them transparent, like windows or images through which a world more substantial than they are can be glimpsed. That world can become visible only through them. The early Gnostics’ reading of Scripture was not mere allegory either. And despite all the differences between ancient Gnosis and Islamic forms of inner knowledge, the Shiite interpretation of the Qur’an is no more reducible to allegory than theirs was.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00931

On this point it has yet to receive anything like fair treatment. Direct awareness of the original events beyond ordinary history goes hand in hand with this gnostic way of knowing. To force it to submit to the standards of historical consciousness would be to do violence to it. We have already heard the Fifth Imam warn that treating the Sacred Book in that way would bring about its death, because it would destroy the spiritual meaning that is always coming to life anew.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00932

This is why I find it deeply troubling to hear people speak of the “errors” of Gnosis. Such judgments silently take as their standard the rationally stated doctrines that would prevail only in later centuries. Anyone who tries to understand Gnosis as a religious phenomenon, in its many forms, will meet one surprise after another.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00933

We must ask what lies behind the vehemence with which Gnosis was attacked during Christianity’s first centuries—a hostility that returns again and again whenever the gnostic spirit reappears. One measure of the alarm it provokes is the response to Origen. He is a Christian teacher whose name can scarcely be mentioned without also raising the question of Gnosis, despite which—or perhaps because of which—he is so often invoked. It is difficult simply to dismiss those who regard him as a Christian Gnostic. He has been criticised for treating the Gospel more as pure spirituality than as historical revelation.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00934

But the opposite criticism could just as fairly be made of his opponents. The clearest sign of Origen’s outlook, we are told, is the apparently insurmountable difficulty he had with the historical fact of the Incarnation.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00935

Yet perhaps the very idea of a “historical fact” had not yet become established in Christian religious consciousness. Perhaps being historical was not, for those early Christians, the test of truth—or perhaps “historical reality” meant something else to them. Certainly the historical Christ, the Christ of the Incarnation and the Passion, caused Origen difficulty.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00936
But why, in turn, were his opponents so angrily disturbed by the pleroma, the heavenly fullness whose “history” the Gnostics told, and by the figures of the Aeon Christ and Sophia?
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00937

Rather than blaming the opposing sides for the beliefs that gave each of them its very reason for being, we would do better to understand what lay behind their positions. Much depends on these unspoken motives, including whether we can grasp the spiritual meaning at issue here.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00938

Throughout Christian history, people with a similar approach to religious experience have shared Origen’s difficulty. They have tended to ask questions that conflict with the standards we now apply to historical religion and historical religious events. One might argue that, without the doctrine of the Incarnation as eventually defined by the Church councils—without the idea that divine and human nature are united in the person of Christ—the central object of Christian faith would never have “entered history.”
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00939

Yet there were people who were fully Christian and felt no need to make that claim. The need arose only once a particular view of history had been accepted: one that made entry into the record of historical events a condition of something’s truth and reality.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00940

Are we to conclude that Christianity itself necessarily gave rise to the historical outlook we hold today? The fact remains that some Christians rejected this requirement and did not find it self-evident. Take the Cross of Light. It is not an event of ordinary history in the way that the Church councils understood the Incarnation.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00941

But for the Gnostics who wrote the Acts of John, the Cross of Light was no less real or true than the cross on Calvary. In fact, it was more real, because they regarded it as the true Cross. This was a real event, but not one that could be witnessed through the physical senses, regardless of the witness’s inner spiritual condition. It belonged to a reality outside the chain of material events that historians study.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00942

Here lies the distinction we need to understand: between a theophany, an appearance or manifestation of God, and an incarnation, God taking on human nature. It is also the distinction between a Gnostic way of understanding religion and a historical one.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00943
Real events take place in the Pleroma, the fullness of the heavenly world. Their nature, time, and place are not those of events as conceived by official Church doctrine.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00944

Yet centuries of thinking historically have made us so dependent on the evidence of outward history that, if a religious event loses its claim to material historical reality, we are inclined to think it has lost all reality. From a Gnostic point of view, this is precisely the danger. When people dismiss spiritual knowledge, ridicule the Pleroma, or deny the reality of the beings and events within it, they may be turning Christianity itself into something merely natural and worldly.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00945

Worse still, by restricting earthly events to the limits of historical fact, they rob those events of their deeper substance and make even Redemption a secular idea. So when the Gnostics are accused of having posed the greatest threat to early Christianity, we should remember that they saw matters in exactly the opposite way. For them, it was their opponents who were placing Christianity in mortal danger.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00946

These disagreements were so serious that the heavenly, spiritual meaning cherished by the Gnostics eventually became confused with—or lost beneath—a safer practice of religious allegory. That practice offered a way to bridge the gap between outward, historical Christianity and the Christianity of inner experience without risking a charge of heresy.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00947

But when we encounter Gnosis again in Islam, we also encounter the idea of a real Event that can be experienced without having to become a material event in history. As we have seen, and will see again, Islam began from a different position. Its prophetic calling rests on experiences of divine manifestation; the Qur’an’s understanding of Christ has affinities with that found in the Acts of John; and an appearance can remain a genuine Event, grounded in a reality that precedes the heavenly world as we know it. This did not spare Islamic mystics the troubles faced by their counterparts elsewhere.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00948

But the circumstances were different. We have tried to show what that difference meant for the spiritual struggle of Shiism. It also makes us consider the upheaval that our modern historical outlook, with its philosophy of history, may bring to a religious consciousness that never shared its assumptions—a consciousness that believed in this world only because it also believed in its end, in both senses of the word: that the world is finite, and that it has a purpose.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00949

Earlier, I suggested that the strict limits placed on harmless allegorical interpretation, wherever it was still allowed alongside the literal and historical meaning of scripture, went hand in hand with the suppression of freely inspired, prophetic interpretation. Those who see the suppression of the Montanist movement in the second century as a decisive turning point in Christianity are probably right. Montanus and his followers claimed that angels were bringing new revelations. They were rejected as heretics who threatened the teaching handed down by the apostles.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00950

From then on, fresh expressions of the Spirit—whether through prophetic messages, visions, or new prophetic readings of earlier revelations—were no longer permitted. The institution of the Church, with its authority to define doctrine, took the place of free prophetic inspiration. Could we say that such inspiration simply “continued” in another form? It seems more accurate to admit that the Church could not accommodate prophecy that spoke freely, or spontaneous revelations of the Spirit.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00951

Tradition therefore had to become fixed in the words of doctrine. The ending of prophetic inspiration, the removal of Gnosis, and the exclusion or destruction of writings labelled apocryphal that had emerged in Gnostic circles—some of them rediscovered only recently—all point in the same direction. They reveal, with striking consistency, the demands of a historically grounded religious outlook in its conflict with the Gnostic outlook.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00952

Other consequences followed. The history of Church doctrines came to be treated as a one-way process. Once Church authorities condemned a teaching as heresy, it belonged to the past. It had supposedly failed to follow the “course of history,” understood as the development of official doctrine. It had been superseded, and there was no reason to reconsider it as a living interpretation that might still challenge us.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00953

At most, scholars could study it as a doctrine of an earlier age. And they could do so without challenging whether it had been orthodox in its own time: after all, it would make little sense to condemn it by appealing to standards that had not yet been established.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00954

But the history of doctrine no longer had any obligation to recognise or respond to signs that speak to us now and might call everything into question. It could only present such writings to present-day readers with a suitably modest air of “objectivity,” showing them the doctrines “as they appear.” Fair enough.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00955

But to whom do they appear? We may refuse to ask, but then we miss the central problem of interpretation. Meaning is never simply there on its own; something has meaning only for someone to whom it speaks. What meaning can a spiritual history hold today for someone who believes it has long since been left behind?
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00956

We do not find the same pattern in traditional Islam. As we already know, a central teaching of Shiism is that the end of the cycle of prophets who bring religious laws opens a new cycle: one devoted to discovering the hidden meanings of divine revelations. This is the cycle of walayat, the spiritual guidance and closeness to God associated with the Imams.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00957

Our authors will show us that, under this name, a hidden or inner prophetic function continues in Islam (nobowwat batina). It is a kind of contemplative prophecy through which inspiration carries on in its own distinct forms (see Chapter V below).
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00958

Spiritual seekers also understand the mystic’s calling and experience through the model of prophetic experience, as a renewal of the gift once granted to the prophets. The walayat of the Imams—their appointment as “people of God,” God’s friends and beloved ones (Awliya Allah)—cannot be compared to the authority of a senior priesthood.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00959

Indeed, the Imamate is now in a state of concealment, or ghaybat. Nor are Muslim writers who catalogue heresies historians of doctrine in the technical Western sense; an accusation of unbelief (takfir) has never had more than a limited, local effect.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00960

What is striking is the extent to which different schools and systems of thought remain present and alive for an Islamic thinker, always capable of being brought to life again. A doctrine is judged by its relation to a spiritual centre, or “pole,” rather than by where it stands in an assumed evolution of doctrine. These schools and ideas send out signs, and the thinker responds according to his own ability to receive them. They present themselves to him, not to an imagined figure from a dead and superseded past whom he is merely trying to reconstruct.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00961

This brings us to a question that also concerns many contemporary philosophers. It is especially revealing that reflection on Islam should lead us to it. Is it possible to devise a single “scientific” way of examining religious questions that means the same thing to people who possess a capacity for religious experience and to people who do not—to believers and nonbelievers alike? That may be as unrealistic as designing a musical instrument equally useful to musicians and to people who cannot hear differences in musical pitch.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00962
But the question cuts both ways. Does “scientific” have only one meaning? Could a disciplined method of interpreting spiritual, inner meaning also be rigorous, reliable, and valid?
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
en-book-1-ch-4-s4
4. Making Events Historical, or Discovering Their Inner Meaning?
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00963

If this really is a choice between two opposing approaches, it is a choice created by the situation we have just examined. Perhaps we can find a way beyond it by questioning the assumptions and categories that produced it in the first place.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00964
Let us briefly recall how the problem developed in the West.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00965

The Reformation of the sixteenth century has been understood in two very different ways. Some see it as hastening the rise of the historical outlook and, with it, the movement towards a secular world no longer shaped by Christianity.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00966

Others see it as holding the remedy for that movement: the possibility of restoring the prophetic inspiration that had been closed off during Christianity’s first centuries. Martin Luther did describe his years as a monk as a time when he “turned everything into allegory.” Later, he wanted instead to tradere Scripturam simplici sensu—to present Scripture in its plain meaning.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00967

Yet we must not forget that his great early discovery grew out of his own mystical training. This was his understanding of significatio passiva: a meaning received and fulfilled within the believer, through faith, in the event of “justification,” by which the believer is made right with God. From this point of view, the literal sense and the sense concerned with a person’s own spiritual life came together.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00968

The old division of Scripture into four meanings, along with its artificial methods, could be overcome only because meaning had been brought inward. Later Protestant orthodoxy would forget the force of this discovery. Its true heirs were those whom Protestant history calls the “Spirituals”: Sebastian Franck, Valentin Weigel, Caspar Schwenckfeld, the followers of Jacob Boehme, and those inspired by the idea of a Rosicrucian Order promoted in the writings of Johann Valentin Andreae. The Thirty Years’ War would crush the hopes attached to that last movement.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00969

We encounter this same tradition in the “divinatory” or intuitively perceptive approach to interpretation developed by Friedrich D. E. Schleiermacher (1768–1834), the great theologian of German Romanticism. Two things about his work matter especially here.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00970

First, Schleiermacher inspired the philosopher and historian Wilhelm Dilthey to develop an approach to interpretation based on understanding another person’s meaning from within. In doing so, Dilthey offered a positive answer to the question with which we ended the previous section: yes, interpretation of inner meaning can be a disciplined method.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00971

Unfortunately, Dilthey’s approach would become lost in the difficulties of historicism, the belief that everything, including our own understanding, is determined by its place in history. It no longer had a clear direction or a firm point of reference. Today the word hermeneutics, meaning the study and practice of interpretation, is widely used in the human sciences. It is significant that, through Dilthey’s work, this use of the term can be traced back to the problem of interpreting a sacred book.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00972

Second, in our own time, a theological approach has emerged that rejects Schleiermacher’s spirit and fights historicism, yet has ended in a dead end of its own. A Muslim student or researcher is unlikely to be familiar with this particular Western debate. We need to say a little about it, because it matters whenever we compare Christian and Islamic theology or philosophy.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00973

We have just mentioned historicism. Once the historical outlook grows so powerful that philosophers can no longer imagine standing outside history—even their own thoughts being shaped and limited by the age in which they live—they have little choice but to examine human lives as they have been recorded in lasting, accessible works. This was Dilthey’s approach: to look for the inner meaning expressed in those works. Interpretation then becomes a science of understanding, an effort to grasp a meaning that reveals itself only under certain conditions.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00974

Above all, there must already be some connection, in life itself, between the interpreter and what the text is about. There must also be a living connection between the interpreter and the author who speaks about it—a relationship in which the interpreter is already personally involved. Interpretation thus becomes, as it was for the Stoics, a “science of the individual.” Its technical goal is to reach conclusions that can claim objective validity.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00975

But does this not assume that some point of reference can stand beyond history? Certainly, we understand Plato only when we think philosophically alongside him. To do that, though, we must understand what Platonism means. We might say that Platonism belongs to a particular period in the history of philosophy, that the period represents a lost age, or that Plato’s writings are among the “sources” from which we can reconstruct that age. Very well.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00976
But before a work can serve as a source, we have to understand it in a particular way.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00977
We must decide what it means, and even decide what the larger historical subject is for which we are treating it as evidence.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00978

We can then spend forever moving around the “circle of interpretation,” where understanding the part depends on the whole and understanding the whole depends on its parts. Or we can watch the horizon of meaning recede endlessly as the uniform line of chronological time grows longer, with no direction or destination.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00979

The only apparent escape is for some unacknowledged system of metaphysics to declare where history is going. Such a system may conceal even the true name of its promised final outcome. It may decree the meaning of political, social, or cultural change and construct a “dialectic of History”—a supposedly necessary movement of history—which is little more than a secular retelling of Bossuet’s Discourse on Universal History. All the while, it forgets that its own standpoint is just as much a product of its historical circumstances as any other.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00980

In short, once this outward, material sense of history has created the idea of a past that is finished and cannot return, philosophers are left with the conclusion that there is “no common measure between history and truth, between the individual and the idea, between the moment and eternity.” The question remains: “How can truth be historical, and how can history be truth?” This is exactly the question that any Gnostic—in the broadest sense of a seeker of saving spiritual knowledge—can put to someone who rejects Gnosis in the name of historical thinking.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00981

Or rather, this is the question by which the Gnostic challenges the agnostic position that created the dilemma in the first place. Wherever the spirit of Gnosis has survived, as it has in the inner teachings of Islam, it has carried with it the idea of knowledge that saves and of divine appearances in the Pleroma. That survival implies that historical consciousness has not expanded without limit, or that its expansion has been resisted. For a long time, it was common to contrast the supposedly “unhistorical” spirit of ancient Greece with the concern for history found in religions of salvation.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00982
But the word historical is ambiguous here. Being in time does not necessarily mean the same thing as belonging to history in the usual sense.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00983

We will see that the spirituality of Iranian Islam makes precisely this distinction. Its insights into the mystical experience of prophecy already offer an answer to a question that concerns philosophers today: there is a time other than the time of history. It is a real, sacred time in which events take place in an unseen world, and the soul is the place where those events occur (see §5 below).
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00984
Since Hegel, we have been used to separating Nature from History, with History understood as the specifically human world.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00985

But for the Muslim sages (hokama) and seekers of spiritual knowledge (orafa) whom we are studying, both Nature and what we call History belong to the world of change and becoming. Both are subject to the same natural process, or physis.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00986

Philosophers after Hegel may contrast historical time with the changing life of Nature, but from the standpoint of Shiite and Sufi wisdom, their historical time is itself merely another way of making time part of Nature. It is misleading, therefore, to speak of Spirit “falling into time” if by time we simply mean history. We should speak instead of time itself falling into history. Only then can we understand how discovering the inner meaning of things brings about a reversal of time.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00987

Arabic, and Persian after it, have a revealing word for this: hikayat. It means a story or account, but it can also mean an imitation or repetition—as if the historian’s art were closely related to the art of an actor or mime. The point is that every story played out in this visible world imitates events that have already taken place within the soul, “in heaven.” That is why the setting of sacred history—the actions and events of the holy story—cannot be seen with our ordinary senses. Its meaning points to another world.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00988

Behind this idea lies a sense of many different kinds of space, of whole “octaves of universes,” as we discussed earlier (§2). It suggests that the truth of an event must be understood at the level of reality where the event actually takes place. This will be especially important when we reach the Twelfth Imam at the end of this work.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00989

Only spiritual interpretation can preserve the truth of hikayat, the truth of the prophetic stories in the Bible and the Qur’an. It does so by understanding their spiritual meaning at the level and in the kind of time where the events truly occur: the time of a reality beyond ordinary history. Once we understand this, we feel no need to “demythologise” the stories of the Bible or the Qur’an. They may not be history in the everyday sense, like an account of Julius Caesar, but that does not make them myths either.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00990

That is why the work of one contemporary school of theology, associated with Rudolf Bultmann, strikes me as tragic. It understands perfectly well the dead end into which historicism leads, yet it continues to reject the one outlook that could free it from agnosticism—including agnosticism dressed in the most devout and orthodox forms. The theologian is caught in a trap.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00991

We see him surrender to historicism at the very moment he claims to be fighting it, when he insists that Christianity must be “demythologised” (Entmythologisierung), on the grounds that the world pictured in the Bible and its stories is now “outdated.” The confusion goes so far that this theology attributes to myth something that properly belongs to rational doctrinal thinking: the attempt to turn divine action into an object or event within the visible world. We are told that myth must be interpreted in terms of human existence, not the structure of the universe.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00992

But why should one kind of interpretation rule out the other? And why blame Gnosis for something directly opposed to its purpose? We are even told that the Gnostic understanding of Redemption reduces the believer’s existence to something within this world, whereas the New Testament places it outside the world. It is astonishing to see such a deep misunderstanding of the Gnostic Pleroma and the events that occur there, of the soul’s existence before earthly life, and of the boundary—the “cross” (stavros)—that separates the Pleroma from this world.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00993

Would the opponents of Gnosis speak differently if they knew a little more about what Gnosis actually means? For now, the same theology that refuses spiritual knowledge is left with a curious contradiction. It calls Christ’s crucifixion on Calvary a historical event, but denies that the Resurrection is historical because the only traces it left in history are the first disciples’ visions.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00994

This is a remarkable admission of defeat: an inability to imagine that visions might themselves be events in the fullest sense. Such events would have their own reality, time, and place, different from those of ordinary history. They belong to what our Muslim sages call the eighth clime, a realm beyond the seven regions of the physical world. I explored this in earlier work, and we will need the idea again at the end of the present book (Book VII).
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00995

Let us be clear. If it is pointless to search for material historical evidence of the Resurrection—because the material world, from this point of view, is precisely the realm of the dead—then Christ’s Passion, no less than his Resurrection, must also be an event that escapes the limits of outward, material history.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00996

Otherwise, we might as well accept every consequence of Nietzsche’s declaration that “God is dead.” Perhaps this theology has already done so. Earlier, however, we saw the upheaval that this supposedly modern understanding of religion can cause in the soul of a Muslim who still believes.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00997

By contrast, we might turn here to Qur’an 4:156. People will call its understanding of Christ “Docetist,” often without knowing what that means. It is not faith in a phantom or a ghost. It is faith in the reality of a spiritual body (caro spiritualis), whose appearance or manifestation (dokē) can be perceived only through spiritual senses. In this sense, what is called “Docetism” is a theological challenge to the usual idea of knowledge, made from the standpoint of faith alone.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00998

We find this in the Acts of John, mentioned earlier, and in related writings that have survived. These “Gnostic” books were not merely products of learned speculation. Ordinary believers used them because, for them, divine manifestations and visions had the force of real events. If modern theology rejects them, we have to ask whether the claims it makes about realities beyond the end of earthly life may amount to little more than an elaborate argument.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-00999

If discovering the inner meaning of events really follows a compelling need that runs in the opposite direction from the drive to place everything within external history, then we cannot avoid the question raised by this discussion. Must Revelation, by its very nature, be turned into historical events? Or is that only one possible way of understanding it? To refuse the question is to assume the answer in advance.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01000

The challenge rests on an undeniable fact: from the earliest days of Christianity, there were Christians who understood and lived their faith without making its decisive Event depend on the material course of outward history. The language of history is understandable, even necessary, when we speak of events of the soul, because they make up a “history of salvation.”
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01001
But there are two very different ways to understand such a history.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01002

We can recognise it where it truly takes place—in the world of the soul, within the kinds of space and time that belong to that world. Then it is a symbolic history, carrying the uncompromising force of its truth. We may fail to understand a symbol, but we cannot refute it simply as we would an ordinary factual claim.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01003

Or we can project that same history onto the chain of outward events, as though it were just another event among them. Once we have made it material in this way, the dialectic of “historical materialism” can easily claim to overcome it and leave it behind.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01004
Here we return to the heart of the tragedy.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01005
We cannot resolve it through the theological failure we have just examined. Theology may be right to say that the Resurrection cannot be verified by searching for material historical traces.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01006

But before announcing that religion must be “demythologised,” it needs to discover that there is such a thing as spiritual history. At one or several levels above the world familiar to us—like higher octaves in music—there are events and forms of time that are fully real, even though they differ completely from the events we usually call “historical.” The question is not whether an event is real, but at what level of existence it is real.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01007

A little familiarity with Gnosis, or a reading of the Acts of John, is enough to begin seeing the difference. Once we see it, we also discover spiritual time: the time proper to the soul, in which new events can continue to happen even after the age of prophets who bring new religious laws has come to an end.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01008

We will return to what continues in Shiism after that prophetic cycle has closed. Wherever the future remains open—or has to be reopened—to inspired readings of the sacred text, the same experiences occur and the same spiritual callings emerge.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01009
We can therefore see certain parallels between the spiritual histories of Christianity and Islam. These parallels came up more than once in our conversations in Iran.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01010

Consider Joachim of Fiore in the twelfth century. One Easter dawn, he experienced an illumination in which the inner meaning of Scripture was revealed to him. He left the results of that revelation in three major treatises devoted to prophetic interpretation—the spiritual understanding (intelligentia spiritualis) of Scripture.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01011

By a remarkable coincidence of timing, this “prophetic abbot” lived at the same time as the Ismaili proclamation of the Great Resurrection at Alamut in Iran, on 8 August 1164. That proclamation established what its participants understood as purely spiritual Islam. It unfolded less like an ordinary historical event than like a sacred rite in which a mystery becomes present. Joachim’s revelation was bound to create a serious crisis within the medieval Church when later followers tried to make it “enter history” in an outward, literal way.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01012

Yet his central idea continued to echo across the centuries, nourishing many philosophies and theologies of the Paraclete—the divine Spirit understood as guide and comforter. Similar prophetic inspirations emerged among the Pietists of Germany, who could also see themselves as faithful to the early spiritual inspiration of the Reformation. In Jacob Boehme (1575–1624), spiritual vision expanded into a prophetic interpretation of the biblical Creation story, the Mysterium Magnum. Johann Albrecht Bengel (1687–1752) also experienced a sudden illumination that gave him an intuitive grasp of Scripture’s inner meaning.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01013

Another striking example is the great Swedish thinker of divine wisdom, Emanuel Swedenborg (1688–1772). A vision awakened his prophetic calling, and he went on to produce an enormous body of work devoted to interpreting spiritual meaning.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01014
What matters is that, among spiritually minded Christians and Muslims alike, the interpretation of hidden or inner meaning rests on three recurring principles.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01015

There is a strict law of correspondences between worlds. The Ismailis call this the “balancing of worlds” (tawazon al-awalim). The idea is that different worlds reflect and answer one another through symbols. It assumes that these worlds really exist, and that there are several levels from which reality can be understood. These are central features of a Gnostic view of the universe.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01016

Heavenly realities are received according to the state of the person who perceives them. What belongs to the heavenly fullness, or Pleroma, becomes visible through real appearances (apparentiae reales), the outward form (zahir). But the way these appearances are experienced depends on the spiritual condition of the person who encounters them.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01017

Outward events can reveal what happens within the soul. The law of correspondences makes events we see or hear about into transparent symbols of inner events. Indeed, the soul can become aware of what is happening within it only through the revealing power of those symbols.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01018

This has little in common either with the allegorical methods of earlier scriptural interpreters or with the allegories long used by modern scholars of religion to “explain” mythology. Together, these principles reveal a network of connections that becomes visible when consciousness frees itself from the chains of material history—chains it has forged for itself. It can then return to inspired, prophetic interpretation, just as “prophetic philosophy” frees us from accepting ready-made facts as the whole of reality.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01019

There is a way of interpreting history that can escape the dead weight of its own supposedly irreversible past only by imposing a meaning on history from above. And there is a prophetic way of interpretation that leads real but still hidden history back to its source, lifting it to a level utterly beyond our material world and the physical, factual, and social evidence that modern people take as the surest evidence of all. There is historical truth, and there is prophetic truth; historical meaning, and prophetic meaning. Events that belong to a reality beyond ordinary history can be forced into a historical mould.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01020

But there is also a movement in the opposite direction, which can restore what that process has lost: bringing outward events back to their inner meaning. There is the continuous, measurable, uniform time of the physical universe, marked by the movement of the stars.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01021

And there is the inner time of the soul and spirit, proper to events experienced within the soul. This time is measured not by quantity but by the qualities of what happens; it does not unfold as one continuous stream. Medieval teachings about angels already contain a hint of this in the idea of tempus discretum, a kind of time made up of distinct moments.
